title: Why is it called Black Friday?

record.question: Why is it called Black Friday?
record.audience_reason: It is Black Friday today; almost everyone has heard the 'stores get in the black' explanation, and the real origin (police slang about traffic) is a satisfying reversal people repeat.

editorial_contribution.statement: We put the two stories in their real order: Philadelphia police slang for the post-Thanksgiving crush by the early 1960s, the merchants' failed 'Big Friday' rename, and the red-to-black profit story catching on in the late 1980s, and we show the crowd-to-gridlock cause on a miniature street.

record.custom_scene: A paper-cutout downtown street: a shop ledger flips red to black and is stamped CAME LATER; suburban cars stream in and slow, an Army-Navy pennant arrives and the lanes lock; a faceless traffic officer works the corner while jams, accidents and shoplifters pop up and a long-shift clock runs; BLACK FRIDAY is stamped on the street; a BIG FRIDAY banner rises and falls; a two-stop timeline carries the name from early 1960s to late 1980s where the profit backstory is attached.

cover_composition.main_object: gridlocked paper street with a traffic officer and a BLACK FRIDAY stamp

record.sources_and_assumptions: See sources-and-rights.md. Assumptions: 'early 1960s' and 'late 1980s' are the sources' own ranges; we do not claim Philadelphia police were the only or first users of the phrase (a Rochester item from Dec 1, 1961 also has police using it), only that the shopping-day name traces to police slang there. The street is a generic illustration, labeled on screen.
